# Runtime Orchestration Principles {.unnumbered}

Part III bounded what a single action may do. Part IV builds the operating system of the Stochastic Computer, the runtime that carries one trajectory across time, and so builds closure for the horizon exposure of H·S·A. Over many steps and hours of wall-clock time, errors compound, tools time out, processes crash, and the environment drifts underneath the agent. A long horizon also reshapes the other two exposures. It turns state into a durability problem, because what the trajectory knows must survive the process that holds it, and it turns authority into an ordering problem, because some effects cannot be undone once later steps depend on them. Part IV answers both through one object, the record the runtime keeps for each trajectory.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation .callout-principle title="Trajectory-level encapsulation"}

**Invariant**: The unit the runtime schedules, budgets, and protects is the whole trajectory, not the model call. Its identity, context handles, cache pointers, tool grants, and resource use live in one Agent Control Block that the runtime owns, and the trajectory advances only through state transitions that the runtime's guards permit.

**Implication**: Model output never changes lifecycle state directly. The runtime rejects illegal transitions, such as a late tool reply for a canceled trajectory or a tool call proposed while the trajectory waits for approval, and it releases accelerator slots and memory whenever the trajectory waits on a tool or a person.

:::

Owning the record gives the runtime the right to stop a trajectory. It still needs a way to know when to.

::: {#pri-vol3-preemptive-interrupts .callout-principle title="Out-of-band preemption and progress watchdogs"}

**Invariant**: A trajectory cannot be relied on to yield, to stop, or to notice that it has stopped making progress. A looping model can stay live, well formed, and inside every per-call limit while advancing nothing.

**Implication**: The runtime must hold control outside the model. It delivers operator and budget signals at turn boundaries, with only a non-maskable kill allowed to break a turn. It bounds every decode with token and wall-clock ceilings and the whole trajectory with a multi-dimensional budget, and it judges progress from the environment's state rather than from heartbeats or the model's own reports.

:::

A record held only in memory dies with the process that holds it.

::: {#pri-vol3-intent-before-effect .callout-principle title="Intent before effect"}

**Invariant**: A trajectory's authoritative state is its append-only log of what the runtime proposed, authorized, dispatched, and observed. The in-memory Agent Control Block is a projection of that log, and re-invoking the model reproduces none of it.

**Implication**: No external effect may leave the host before the record that authorizes it is durable. Recovery replays the log from the latest snapshot without calling the model or the tools, and an intent with no recorded outcome stays in doubt until it is settled, never re-dispatched on the assumption that it failed.

:::

The log makes the runtime's own state recoverable. The environment's state is another matter.

::: {#pri-vol3-reversibility-sagas .callout-principle title="The pivot boundary and compensating Sagas"}

**Invariant**: Every action is invertible, compensable, or irreversible. An invertible action, such as a write confined to the sandbox, can be undone exactly by rolling back to a snapshot. A compensable action on a shared external system can be answered by another action that restores the environment's invariants but not its history. After an irreversible action the runtime can only complete forward.

**Implication**: The supervisory runtime must register a compensating action for each compensable step before dispatching it, allow at most one irreversible pivot action per trajectory and order it after all compensable work, and gate the pivot with deterministic checks and, where policy requires, a human approval. Once the pivot commits, recovery switches from compensation to idempotent retry or escalation.

:::

@Sec-vol3-agent-harness gives each trajectory an Agent Control Block and a supervisor that can pause, escrow, budget, and stop it without the model's cooperation. @Sec-vol3-durable-execution derives that block from an append-only log so that it survives a crash. @Sec-vol3-failure-recovery repairs the world around it when a multi-step task fails partway. With Part IV in place the live loop is complete, and every closure it provides holds whatever the model's weights happen to be. Part V turns to those weights.
